title: Live Blackjack vs RNG Blackjack: A Canadian Guide
excerpt: Live blackjack or RNG blackjack? A Canadian guide to speed, table limits, rules, side bets, bonus eligibility and which format fits your bankroll best.
author: David Andersen
bodyHtml:
Open the blackjack lobby at a Canadian-facing casino and you are really looking at two different games wearing the same name. On one side sits live blackjack, streamed in real time from a studio with a human dealer and a real shoe. On the other sits RNG blackjack, software where a certified random number generator decides every card. The rules look similar on the felt, but the formats differ enormously in speed, cost, table limits and even whether your bonus counts them at all.

How live blackjack actually works

A live table is a broadcast. A dealer stands at a physical table in a studio and deals from a genuine multi-deck shoe. Cameras cover the table from several angles, and optical card recognition reads each card as it leaves the shoe, turning the physical deal into data that updates your screen and the payout engine instantly.

Your decisions travel the other way. You press hit, stand, double or split inside a fixed window — usually ten to twenty seconds — and the dealer sees those choices on a monitor. Nothing about the shuffle is simulated: cards are shuffled by hand or by machine, and many studios use a continuous shuffler that returns played cards to the shoe immediately.

How RNG blackjack works

RNG blackjack has no physical deck. The software models a shoe of a defined size and uses a random number generator to select cards. Reputable studios have their RNGs tested by independent labs, and regulated markets require certification of the generator and the game's stated return. The virtual shoe reshuffles after every hand, so each deal starts from a full, freshly randomised set.

With no dealer to pay and no studio to run, RNG tables are far cheaper to offer, which shows up in the minimum bet, the range of variants and how fast you can play. For context on the rest of the lobby, our rundown of the main online casino game categories sets blackjack alongside slots and roulette.

Speed of play and why hands per hour matters

Your expected cost is roughly your average bet multiplied by the house edge multiplied by the number of hands played. The house edge gets all the attention, but hands per hour is the term players ignore, and it swings wildest between the two formats.

A live table moves at the pace of a human dealer serving up to seven seats — realistically several dozen hands an hour, fewer at a full table. An RNG game waits for nobody, and a focused player can push several hundred. At identical stakes and rules, RNG blackjack can cost multiples more per hour purely through throughput. The flip side is that if you deliberately slow down, RNG is the cheapest way to log practice hands at tiny stakes.

Table limits and bankroll fit

RNG tables often start at a dollar or less, because an empty table costs nothing to run. Live tables carry studio and staffing overhead, so minimums start higher and climb steeply on VIP tables — though live ceilings are much higher, which is why larger bankrolls gravitate there.

The practical consequence is unit size. If your session budget is a hundred dollars and the cheapest live seat is ten, you have ten units of protection against variance, nowhere near enough for blackjack's swings. The same budget at a one-dollar RNG table gives you a hundred units and a far better chance of surviving a bad run.

Rules that move the house edge

Blackjack's house edge is not fixed. It is assembled from the rule set posted on the table, and those differences are worth more than any betting system ever invented.

3:2 versus 6:5

A natural should pay three to two. Some tables, live and RNG alike, pay six to five instead. That single change costs roughly an extra 1.4 percent of every dollar wagered, often more than the entire house edge of a well-ruled game, with no compensating benefit. If the table says 6:5, leave and find another.

Everything else on the felt

Fewer decks favour the player, so single or double-deck games beat an eight-deck shoe. A dealer standing on soft 17 is better for you than one who hits it. Doubling after a split, doubling on any two cards, re-splitting pairs and late surrender all shave the edge further. A generous rule set can land under half a percent; a mean one is several times that. Our blackjack strategy and rules guide breaks the individual rule costs down further.

Side bets in live blackjack

Live studios lean on side bets because they are profitable and they look exciting. Perfect Pairs pays when your first two cards match, most for an identical suited pair. 21+3 combines your cards with the dealer's up card and pays poker-style results such as a flush, straight or three of a kind. Both are fun, and both carry a house edge many times higher than the main game.

Treat them as entertainment spending, not strategy. A player making careful decisions on a good table while feeding two side bets every hand has thrown away the low edge they worked to get.

Strategy, charts and why counting fails online

Basic strategy is identical in both formats: the correct play for a hard sixteen against a dealer ten is the same whether a human or an algorithm turns the card. Better still, nobody can stop you keeping a strategy chart open beside your screen. There is no pit boss and no social awkwardness, and playing from a chart is the cheapest improvement available to anyone.

Card counting, though, is effectively dead online. RNG games reshuffle after every hand, so no count persists. Live tables increasingly use continuous shufflers, and even with a traditional shoe the penetration is deliberately shallow — the shoe is replaced long before the remaining cards become informative.

Atmosphere, bet behind and multi-seat play

Live tables sell a feeling software cannot: dealers greet players by name, a chat panel runs alongside, and the shared rhythm gives a session shape. Bet behind lets you wager on a seated player's hand when the table is full, which gets you into a busy game but hands your decisions to a stranger. Multi-seat play lets you occupy two or three seats at once, raising hands per hour and exposure at the same rate.

Connection, data and disconnection rules

Live blackjack is video, so it uses real bandwidth — enough to matter on a capped Canadian mobile plan, and a long session on cellular data can run into gigabytes. RNG games are light and tolerate patchy connections.

Disconnection handling differs too. If your connection drops mid-hand at a live table the dealer will not wait; house rules normally stand your hand once the timer expires, a poor outcome on a hand you meant to hit or double. RNG games generally hold the state and return you to the decision point. Check the policy in the game rules, and stay on stable Wi-Fi for live play.

Bonus eligibility and wagering requirements

This catches Canadians out constantly. Blackjack's low house edge makes it unattractive as bonus turnover, so it usually contributes very little toward wagering requirements — often a small percentage, sometimes nothing, against full contribution for slots. Many bonus terms go further and exclude live dealer games entirely, meaning those wagers count for zero and may void the offer.

Read the game contribution table before claiming anything you intend to play blackjack with. Operators that publish those terms plainly deserve preference, and our PlayOJO casino review shows what transparency should look like. For serious blackjack, a small cash promotion or no bonus at all often beats a large slots-oriented package you can never clear.

Which format suits which Canadian player

  • Small or cautious bankroll: RNG at the lowest stake, played deliberately rather than fast.
  • Learning basic strategy: RNG, with a chart open, because repetition is cheap and there is no decision timer.
  • Wants atmosphere and a social hour: live, at the lowest table you can fund for your intended session length.
  • Larger bankroll or higher stakes: live, where ceilings are high and rules are clearly posted.
  • On mobile data or a shaky connection: RNG, every time.
  • Clearing a bonus: probably neither — check contribution rates first.

A practical checklist before you sit down

  • Confirm blackjack pays 3:2, not 6:5, and leave if it does not.
  • Check the deck count and whether the dealer hits or stands on soft 17.
  • Confirm double after split, doubling on any two cards, re-splitting and surrender.
  • Set a session budget and a unit size of roughly one to two percent of it per hand.
  • Decide your side bet policy in advance, ideally zero.
  • Have your basic strategy chart open before the first hand.
  • Read the disconnection rule for that specific table.
  • Check bonus contribution and whether live tables are excluded.
  • Set a time limit as well as a money limit, because hands per hour drives real cost.

Both formats are legitimate and both can be played well; the mistake is assuming they are interchangeable. Live tables are slower, richer and more expensive per seat, while RNG is cheaper to enter, faster if you let it be, and far more forgiving of a modest bankroll.
